title: Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law
description: 'Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law' is the ten-part title poem of Adrienne Rich's third collection, Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law: Poems 1954-1962 (Harper & Row, 1963), the book in which she broke with the formal, Audenesque verse of A Change of World and The Diamond Cutters and began to write the poem of her own life. Written over three years while she was raising three sons in Cambridge, Massachusetts, it is a sequence of scenes of women - a daughter-in-law at the sink, a mother-in-law, Emily Dickinson, Mary Wollstonecraft - held together by a voice that moves between them, and it is the first poem in which Rich's feminism becomes a poetic method rather than a subject.
plot_or_argument: The poem is a sequence of 'snapshots', and its method is montage: each section holds a scene or a quotation for a moment and then cuts to the next, so that the reader has to supply the argument that connects them. Section one gives us two women screaming at one another across cut glass and majolica, 'cornered from their prey', and makes their quarrel a quarrel between a woman and the image of herself that her world has given her. Section two gives us the domestic interior and the daughter-in-law's self-harm at the sink, which is also an act of privacy, and the mother whose mind is 'mouldering like wedding-cake' - the marriage plot arriving as decay. The middle sections turn to the women writers who lived the same contradiction: Dickinson, who wrote in her father's house, Wollstonecraft, and the medieval Christine, whose learning was counted against her. The poem's quotations of male poets are not simply rejected; they are answered, turned inside out, so that 'ma semblable, ma soeur' becomes a description of the relation between women rather than a sneer. What the sequence argues, without stating it, is that the entrapment of the daughter-in-law in her kitchen and the achievement of the woman writer are the same history seen at different distances. The ending opens the prison-house doors but does not say what is outside them, and that hesitation is the poem's honesty.
narrative_structure: Ten numbered sections of unequal length, in free verse with a strong rhythmic organisation by phrase and by repetition rather than by metre; sections juxtapose the contemporary domestic scene with historical and literary material, and the transitions are made by image rather than by argument. Quotation is set into the verse without quotation marks, so that the poem's 'own' voice and its borrowed voices are not clearly separated.
meter_and_prosody: Long, irregular lines whose measure is rhetorical rather than metrical; a syntax that runs over the line break and often over the stanza break; dense imagery drawn from domestic objects and from myth; quotation and near-quotation of other writers; a tone that moves from the satiric to the elegiac within a section; an undercurrent of bodily disgust and of desire for escape.
historical_context: Written between 1958 and 1960, while Rich was living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, married to the economist Alfred Conrad and raising three small sons, and published in Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law: Poems 1954-1962 (New York: Harper & Row, 1963). She later wrote that the book had taken her three years to write and six to publish, that the Times ignored it after praising her first two books, and that her father called the poems 'sordid, irritable and often nasty'. It appeared the year after The Feminine Mystique, and is one of the first books of American poetry to register the dissatisfaction that book described.
literary_significance: 'Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law' is the poem in which Adrienne Rich's feminism becomes visible and the book from which her later poetry is usually dated; it is a standard anthology text in courses on postwar American poetry and on women's writing, and it is one of the poems through which the origins of second-wave feminist poetry in the United States are taught. Its montage method - the historical fragment beside the contemporary kitchen - became one of the standard procedures of feminist poetry in the 1970s.
bibliographical_notes: Collected as the title poem of Snapshots of a Daughter-in-Law: Poems 1954-1962 (New York: Harper & Row, 1963); reprinted in Collected Early Poems 1950-1970 (1993) and in Adrienne Rich's Poetry and Prose (Norton Critical Edition, 1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the relation between a woman's domestic life and her intellectual life, and it refuses the choice the culture offers between them: the daughter-in-law scalds herself at the sink, and the poet quotes Dickinson. Its second subject is the tradition of women's writing, which the poem constructs as a set of precursors - Dickinson, Wollstonecraft, Christine - who are present in the same poem as the dishes. Its third is enclosure and its figures: the trunk, the pantry, the cage, the vault. The violence of the language - Furies, prey, flies, knives - makes the poem's account of domesticity anything but gentle, and its ending holds out a release that it refuses to describe.
summary: The sequence moves through ten numbered sections. The first presents two handsome women 'gripped in argument', 'like Furies cornered from their prey', and the second the daughter-in-law at her dishes, who scalds herself deliberately and thinks of her mother, whose mind is 'mouldering like wedding-cake'; she resolves 'to be another way'. Later sections quote and answer a masculine tradition - Baudelaire's 'ma semblable, ma soeur' is turned against him - and bring in Emily Dickinson, writing letters in her father's house, and Mary Wollstonecraft, and the fifteenth-century poet Christine de Pisan. The poem's images are those of enclosure: a 'commodious steamer-trunk', a pantry, a birdcage, a vault, a 'mail of the mind'. It ends with a winter landscape and a voice that is no longer sure whether it is the daughter-in-law's or the poet's, and with the line 'the doors of the prison-house stand open'.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as a transitional work between the formal early Rich and the political later Rich, as an early instance of feminist montage, and as a poem divided against itself in ways that are thematically productive; the question of its relation to the confessional poetry of Lowell and Sexton has been discussed at length, since Rich's 'I' is historical rather than therapeutic. Its treatment of Dickinson in particular has been central to the feminist criticism of the 1970s and after.
research_notes: The first periodical printing of the poem was not established from the sources consulted, so the record dates it from its first book appearance in 1963, which is the date the anthology gives. The text was read through the printed extracts and the critical accounts consulted; quotations are short.

title: "I Am in Danger—Sir—"
description: 'I Am in Danger-Sir-' is a short poem in the voice of Emily Dickinson, collected in Adrienne Rich's Necessities of Life: Poems 1962-1965 (W. W. Norton, 1966). Its title is a quotation from Dickinson's letters to Thomas Wentworth Higginson, the man of letters who became her correspondent and who advised her not to publish; the poem takes that sentence and gives it back as a declaration, so that the poet's famous seclusion and her refusal of the literary market become an assertion of authority.
plot_or_argument: The poem is a monologue of some twenty lines in which Rich inhabits Dickinson and answers her editor. Its occasion is the correspondence with Higginson that began in 1862, when Dickinson wrote to him asking whether her verse was 'alive', and continued until her death; Higginson's advice, in effect, was to wait, to regularise her metre, and not to publish. Rich's poem takes his intervention as the type of all masculine mediation of women's writing and answers it from inside Dickinson's own vocabulary - the house, the room, the garden, the letter, the 'Balm' and the 'Bee'. The title's quotation is the poem's argument: Dickinson's declaration of danger, written to the man who had offered to protect her, is reread as a claim to the risk that writing is. The poem does not narrate; it asserts, and it ends on an assertion that is also a refusal - the refusal of the terms on which genius was to be licensed.
narrative_structure: A single short poem without stanza divisions in most printings, in short free-verse lines that echo Dickinson's hymn measure without adopting it; a dramatic monologue spoken throughout by Dickinson, with no frame and no narrator's commentary. The title is part of the poem: it supplies the addressee and the quotation that the body of the poem answers.
meter_and_prosody: Short lines, abrupt syntax and heavy dashes in Dickinson's manner, used sparingly rather than imitated; a diction of the household and of the garden; capitalised abstractions; a rhetorical structure of assertion and withdrawal; a voice that is cool, ironic and absolute by turns.
historical_context: Collected in Necessities of Life: Poems 1962-1965 (New York: W. W. Norton, 1966), the book written during Rich's years of anti-war and civil rights activism, when her marriage was under strain and her poetry was moving from the formal verse of her first two books to the documentary and political manner of The Will to Change. The poem belongs to the same period as 'When We Dead Awaken: Writing as Re-Vision' (1971), in which Rich argued that women must reread the literary tradition in order to write at all.
literary_significance: 'I Am in Danger-Sir-' is a standard text in the feminist criticism of the 1960s and 1970s and one of the earliest poems in which a twentieth-century woman poet enters the voice of a nineteenth-century one in order to argue with the institution that mediated her; it is anthologised in the Norton anthologies and in collections of American women's poetry, and it prepared the ground for Rich's own later work on Dickinson, including her editions of the fascicles and her essay 'Vesuvius at Home'.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in Necessities of Life: Poems 1962-1965 (New York: W. W. Norton, 1966); reprinted in Collected Early Poems 1950-1970 (1993) and in Adrienne Rich's Poetry and Prose (Norton Critical Edition, 1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the relation of a woman writer to her editor and to the literary institution he represents, and it reads Dickinson's seclusion not as pathology but as a choice about the conditions of work. Its second subject is the materiality of writing - paper scraps, letters, the room - which Rich, later a great editor of Dickinson's manuscripts, insists on. Its third is aesthetics: the poem is an argument, made in Dickinson's own compressed measure, that the formal strangeness for which she was criticised is the mark of the poetry's life.
summary: The poem addresses a 'Sir' - Higginson, the editor and critic, and, behind him, the whole apparatus of publication and taste - and answers his advice. It speaks in Dickinson's voice about the conditions of her writing: the house, the garden, the room upstairs, the poems written on scraps of paper, the letters that were her public. It refuses the terms in which she was offered help, and it claims for her work the very danger that the phrase in the title mentions, so that 'I am in danger, sir' becomes not a confession of female fragility but a statement about what the writing is. It is short, compressed and epigrammatic in Dickinson's manner.
critical_context: Critics have read the poem as a founding instance of the feminist practice of 'writing back' to the tradition, as an intervention in the editing and reception of Dickinson, and as a poem about the institutional mediations - editors, letters, publication - that surround a woman's text. Its relation to Rich's later essay on Dickinson, and to the feminist recovery of Dickinson's manuscripts, has been widely discussed.
research_notes: The first periodical printing was not established from the sources consulted; the poem is dated from its collection in 1966, which is the date the anthology gives. The title's quotation from Dickinson's letters is given in the anthology's punctuation.

title: A Valediction Forbidding Mourning
description: 'A Valediction Forbidding Mourning' is the poem of Adrienne Rich's The Will to Change: Poems 1968-1970 (W. W. Norton, 1971) that most directly confronts the literary tradition: it takes its title from John Donne's famous poem of parting and answers it, in a woman's voice, about the impossibility of using a language that has been made by and for men. It belongs to the years of Rich's divorce, of her anti-war activism and of the essays that became 'When We Dead Awaken', and it is one of the first poems in which she makes the critique of language itself her subject.
plot_or_argument: The poem's occasion is a parting, but its subject is the language in which a parting can be said. Donne's 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning' consoles two lovers by comparing their souls to the twin legs of a drafting compass, one fixed at the centre and one travelling the circle back to it; Rich's poem takes the same instrument and makes it an image of the constraint under which a woman writes, so that the circle that Donne meant as fidelity becomes the closed circuit of a tradition that returns every woman's sentence to its origin in a man's. The poem's short lines refuse the discursive ease of its model: where Donne argues, Rich asserts and then withdraws, and the syntax is broken so that the reader has to supply the connections. Its repeated words - 'the thing', 'the enemy', 'the tongue' - make it a poem about naming, and its refusal to name the beloved directly is part of its argument about what a woman's love poem can and cannot say in the inherited forms. The ending neither consoles nor wins; it records the condition of writing against a language one cannot do without.
narrative_structure: A short free-verse poem in irregularly broken lines, with no stanza divisions in most printings; its argument is made by the juxtaposition of the inherited conceit and a contemporary voice that cannot use it. The title announces its relation to Donne and the poem does not explain the relation, so that the reader's recognition is part of the poem's method.
meter_and_prosody: Short lines broken at the point of syntactic strain; a vocabulary of instruments and of the body; repetition of a small number of charged words; a refusal of the simile and the conceit that the poem is criticising, so that the poem's own figures are minimal; a tone that is cold, exact and finally unresolved.
historical_context: Collected in The Will to Change: Poems 1968-1970 (New York: W. W. Norton, 1971), the book written during Rich's divorce, her activism against the Vietnam War and her turn to feminism; it is contemporary with the essay 'When We Dead Awaken: Writing as Re-Vision' (1971), in which she argued that women must re-read the tradition 'with new eyes' in order to write. The title alludes to Donne's 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning', first printed in 1633.
literary_significance: The poem is the standard exhibit in accounts of Rich's turn to the critique of language and of the literary tradition, and it is anthologised as one of the first American poems to make the answer to a canonical male text its formal principle; it is regularly taught beside Donne's poem and beside the essays of 'When We Dead Awaken', and it belongs to the small group of poems through which the feminist practice of revisionist reading was established in the 1970s.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in The Will to Change: Poems 1968-1970 (New York: W. W. Norton, 1971); reprinted in Collected Early Poems 1950-1970 (1993) and in Adrienne Rich's Poetry and Prose (Norton Critical Edition, 1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the politics of the literary tradition: the recognition that the forms and metaphors a poet inherits carry the assumptions of the society that made them, and that a woman writer's relation to them is therefore never neutral. Its second subject is the possibility of a love poetry that is not founded on the exchange of one person into another's figure. Its third is the practical experience of writing in the early 1970s, when Rich was making, in her poetry and her essays, the argument that a woman must reread and rewrite the tradition in order to write at all.
summary: The poem begins with a refusal of the metaphor by which Donne's lovers are joined: it speaks of the difficulty of writing at all, of 'the thing I came for', and of a language that is 'the enemy'. Its images are of maps, tools and instruments, of the 'tongue of the past', of the 'spike' and the 'compass', and it quotes and reverses the terms of Donne's conceit so that the circle drawn by the compass becomes a trap rather than a proof of union. The poem is short, compressed, and ends on the recognition that the words available to it are 'the enemy's' words, and that the poem must use them anyway.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as an example of 're-vision' in the sense Rich gave the word, as an intervention in the metaphysical tradition, and as a poem about the difficulty of writing love poetry in a political moment; its relation to Donne's conceit, and to the question of whether a poem can criticise the language it uses, has been extensively discussed.
research_notes: The first periodical printing was not established from the sources consulted; the poem is dated from its collection in 1971, which is the date the anthology gives. The record shares its title with Donne's poem but is a distinct work.

title: Diving into the Wreck
description: 'Diving into the Wreck' is the title poem of Adrienne Rich's seventh book, Diving into the Wreck: Poems 1971-1972 (W. W. Norton, 1973), and the poem through which her middle period is known. It describes a scuba diver descending to a wreck, with a book of myths in which the diver's name does not appear, in order to see the damage that was done and the treasures that prevail; it turns the descent into an allegory of the woman writer's relation to history. The book won the National Book Award for Poetry in 1974, which Rich refused as an individual and accepted, with Audre Lorde and Alice Walker, on behalf of all women.
plot_or_argument: The poem's narrative is a dive, described with technical precision and without allegorical pointing. The diver dresses - the rubber suit, the flippers, the mask, the knife - and the equipment is insisted on as equipment, absurd and necessary, before it becomes a figure for anything. The descent is a passage out of one medium into another: the sea is 'another story', the ladder descends from the schooner into water that does not change, and the diver's breathing is audible all the way down. The wreck appears first as a shadow and then as a structure, and the exploration of it is an exploration of a ruined household: the cabin, the cargo, the 'silver, copper, vermeil cargo', the drowned faces. The poem's central recognition is that the diver has come to see the damage and not the myth, and that the book of myths in which the divers' names do not appear is nonetheless carried along. Its most famous lines dissolve the distinction between the selves - 'I am she: I am he' - and the wreck's survivor becomes both the woman and the man, the drowned and the living, so that the poem's allegory, if it has one, is about the recovery of a common history rather than a separate one. The ending refuses both rescue and consolation: the diver is in the wreck, among the tools and the corrosion, and that is where the poem leaves her.
narrative_structure: Ten numbered sections, in free verse, whose sequence follows the dive: the equipment, the descent, the approach, the wreck, the cabin, the cargo, the recognition, the ending. The sections are held together by repetition of phrases from section to section ('the sea is another story', 'the book of myths') and by the persistence of the second person, so that the poem addresses a companion who is also the reader and also the self.
meter_and_prosody: Long unrhymed lines with a strong caesura and a prose-like clarity; technical vocabulary used literally and only then figuratively; repetition of whole sentences as refrain; a second-person address that shifts its object; almost no simile in the dive itself, so that the allegory is carried by the narrative rather than by ornament.
historical_context: Written in 1972 and collected in Diving into the Wreck: Poems 1971-1972 (New York: W. W. Norton, 1973), the book that followed Rich's divorce, her move to New York and her increasing involvement in the women's movement; it won the National Book Award for Poetry in 1974, a prize she declined as an individual and accepted jointly with Audre Lorde and Alice Walker 'on behalf of all women', a gesture that became a defining moment of second-wave feminist literary politics. The poem's wreck is not any particular ship; the dive is a figure for the encounter with a history that has been submerged.
literary_significance: 'Diving into the Wreck' is the central poem of Rich's middle period and one of the most influential American poems of the 1970s; its images - the body-armour, the book of myths, the wreck - have become part of the common vocabulary of feminist criticism, and the National Book Award gesture made the poem and its book a public event. It is a standard anthology text in courses on postwar American poetry, women's writing and the literature of the 1970s.
bibliographical_notes: Collected as the title poem of Diving into the Wreck: Poems 1971-1972 (New York: W. W. Norton, 1973); reprinted in Poems: Selected and New, 1950-1974 (1974) and in Adrienne Rich's Poetry and Prose (Norton Critical Edition, 1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the relation of the present to a damaged past, and it makes the dive a method: to go down to the wreck is to refuse the available versions of history and to look at the damage directly. Its second subject is gender, and its treatment of it is deliberately unsettling: the diver, 'she who is me', becomes 'he' in the wreck and the wreck's survivor is 'I am she: I am he', which makes the poem an argument about the commonness of the catastrophe rather than a separate women's history. Its third subject is the book of myths in which the divers' names do not appear - the written record that has excluded them - and the poem's own relation to it, since the poem is itself a book that names them.
summary: The poem is in ten sections. It begins with the preparation of the diver - 'I put on / the body-armor of black rubber, / the absurd flippers, / the grave and awkward mask' - and the descent, which is also a descent out of the ordinary social world: 'the sea is another story'. The diver descends a ladder that 'hangs / from the side of the schooner' into water that is 'the same as always'. The wreck appears, and the diver explores its cabin, its cargo, its instruments, finding 'the thing itself and not the myth'. The poem's most quoted lines describe the diver as 'she who is me' and the creature in the wreck as 'I am she: I am he', a merging of the sexes in the figure of the survivor. The book of myths, in which 'our names do not appear', is carried down and remains, and the poem ends in the wreck's cabin, among its treasures and its damage.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as an allegory of feminist historiography, as a rewriting of the descent narratives of epic and of psychoanalysis, and as a poem whose dissolving of gender - 'I am she: I am he' - has been central to the debate about essentialism in feminist poetics. Its relation to Rich's essays of the same years, and to the work of Adrienne Rich's contemporaries among women poets, has been extensively discussed.
research_notes: The first periodical printing was not established from the sources consulted; the poem is dated from its collection in 1973, which is the date the anthology gives. The book's fifth printing is sometimes dated 1975 in library records; 1973 is the first edition.

title: Power
description: 'Power' is the poem that opens Adrienne Rich's The Dream of a Common Language: Poems 1974-1977 (W. W. Norton, 1978), the first book she published after coming out as a lesbian in 1976. It is a short poem in five couplets about Marie Curie, who discovered polonium and radium and died of the radiation that made her famous, and it reads her life as a parable of the cost at which women have been permitted power. It is one of Rich's most quoted poems and the clearest statement of the book's argument about power, gender and knowledge.
plot_or_argument: The poem works as a diptych. Its first movement uncovers the past as an excavation: 'living in the earth-deposits of our history', the speaker watches a backhoe split open the ground and reveal a bottle, amber and perfect, 'a hundred-year-old cure for fever or melancholy', a tonic 'for living on this earth / in the winters of this climate'. The bottle is a woman's remedy, a domestic medicine, and the poem treats it without condescension: it is a real attempt at relief, made by someone whose name is not recorded. The second movement names Marie Curie, who 'died a famous woman denying / her wounds / denying / her wounds came from the same source as her power'. The lines have the flatness of an epitaph, and their force comes from the double denial: Curie denied that the radium was killing her, and the world has denied that her achievement and her destruction were one thing. The poem does not resolve the relation between the anonymous herbalist and the Nobel laureate; it sets them side by side as two women who worked with what the earth contained, and it asks the reader to see that the difference between them is a difference in public record rather than in kind.
narrative_structure: Five unrhymed couplets, with a turn between the third and fourth: the first three couplets are the excavation and the tonic, the last two are Curie and her denial. The poem's brevity is part of its argument; it offers no explanation of the connection it draws, and its two halves are held together only by the phrase 'earth-deposits' and by the idea of a substance that both heals and harms.
meter_and_prosody: Short, flat, declarative lines; a couplet form that sets two statements against each other; a diction that mixes the archaeological and the medical ('earth-deposits', 'backhoe', 'tonic', 'melancholy'); a deliberate refusal of metaphor in the Curie section, where the plainest possible statement is the most damning; repetition ('denying / her wounds / denying') used to make the denial visible.
historical_context: Collected in The Dream of a Common Language: Poems 1974-1977 (New York: W. W. Norton, 1978), the first book Rich published after coming out as a lesbian in 1976 and the book in which she began to write explicitly for a community of women; its three sections - 'Power', 'Twenty-One Love Poems' and 'Not Somewhere Else, But Here' - are organised around the question the title announces. Marie Curie (1867-1934) won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and in Chemistry in 1911 and died of aplastic anaemia caused by radiation exposure; her notebooks remain radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes.
literary_significance: 'Power' is one of the most anthologised poems of Rich's later work and the standard text for her argument about women, knowledge and cost; its lines about Curie are among the most quoted in American feminist poetry, and the poem is central to the teaching of The Dream of a Common Language and of the poetry of the women's movement of the 1970s.
bibliographical_notes: Opens The Dream of a Common Language: Poems 1974-1977 (New York: W. W. Norton, 1978); reprinted in Adrienne Rich's Poetry and Prose (Norton Critical Edition, 1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the cost of women's power and the way that cost is written out of the record: Curie's fame depends on the denial of her wounds, and the anonymous maker of the tonic is not famous at all. Its second subject is knowledge as a physical practice - the backhoe, the bottle, the lead-lined notebooks - and the body as the instrument and the casualty of that practice. Its third is history itself, figured as stratified earth that has to be excavated: the 'earth-deposits of our history' contain both the cure and the poison, and the poem refuses to choose between them.
summary: The poem's first image is an archaeological one: the speaker has been 'living in the earth-deposits of our history', and a backhoe has uncovered a bottle of 'a hundred-year-old cure for fever or melancholy' - a tonic, a patent medicine, an old promise of relief. The poem then turns to Marie Curie, 'denying / her wounds / denying / her wounds came from the same source as her power'. The final image is of Curie's hands, and of the notebooks that are still radioactive and must be kept in lead-lined boxes. The poem's argument is carried by the juxtaposition of the two women: the anonymous maker of the tonic and the famous scientist, both of whom worked with the substances of the earth and both of whom paid for it in the body.
critical_context: Critics have read the poem as an exemplary feminist history, as a critique of the ideology of scientific heroism, and as a poem about the materiality of knowledge; its pairing of Curie with an anonymous maker of patent medicine has been discussed as a model of Rich's practice of constructing a women's tradition out of the surviving record. Its relation to the rest of The Dream of a Common Language has been extensively analysed.
research_notes: The first periodical printing was not established from the sources consulted; the poem is dated from its collection in 1978, which is the date the anthology gives.

title: Transcendental Etude
description: 'Transcendental Etude' is the final poem of Adrienne Rich's The Dream of a Common Language: Poems 1974-1977 (W. W. Norton, 1978), and the long meditation in which the book's argument about art, women and a common language is gathered up. Its title takes the name of Liszt's piano studies and turns it against virtuosity: what the poem asks for is not transcendence or brilliance but a 'composition' made of ordinary materials by a woman in a room, and its closing lines - about a whole new poetry beginning 'here' - are among the most quoted in Rich's work.
plot_or_argument: 'Transcendental Etude' is a long poem in loosely broken free verse paragraphs, and it is structured as a meditative walk: it begins outdoors, among birches and hills, and the walk turns into thinking, and the thinking turns into a room and an act of making. The poem's opening is a refusal of the heroic vocabulary of art - it will not strive for 'greatness, brilliance' - and it proposes instead a 'composition' that has to do with a mind 'one with her body' and with 'care for the many-lived, unending / forms in which she finds herself'. From this it moves to the history of women, to the recognition that 'in fact we were always like this, / rootless, dismembered: knowing it makes the difference', and to the materials of a women's tradition: the quilt, the cloth, the hands that have made things out of what was available. The poem's last movement is domestic and precising: two women in a room, one making something, the other watching, and the poem ends by naming what they are doing as 'a whole new poetry beginning here'. The 'here' is deliberately unglamorous - a rented room, a kitchen, a table - and the poem's argument is that the beginning of a common language is a material practice rather than a revelation.
narrative_structure: A single continuous poem in verse paragraphs of varying length, without numbered sections; its movements are a walk, a meditation, a history and a scene, connected by association and by the recurrence of a few images - the hills, the birches, the room, the hands, the cloth. It is the longest poem in the book and it is placed last, so that it functions as the book's conclusion.
meter_and_prosody: Long, unrhymed, heavily enjambed lines that move at the pace of thinking; a syntax of qualification and apposition; a diction that mixes the domestic ('a piece of cloth', 'the rooms we live in') with the philosophical ('transcendence', 'composition', 'the many-lived'); quotation of the title's musical form as an irony; a closing line that turns on a single deictic, 'here'.
historical_context: Written in the mid-1970s and collected in The Dream of a Common Language: Poems 1974-1977 (New York: W. W. Norton, 1978), the book that followed Rich's coming out and her move into the women's movement; its title alludes to Franz Liszt's Douze études d'exécution transcendante (1851), piano studies of extreme difficulty, and the poem deliberately sets the domestic and the unspectacular against them. The book is dedicated to the idea of a language women might share, and its final poem is the fullest statement of that idea.
literary_significance: 'Transcendental Etude' is the poem in which Rich's later poetics is most fully stated and one of the most widely anthologised American poems of the 1970s; its closing phrase, 'a whole new poetry beginning here', has become a slogan of feminist writing, and the poem is a standard text in courses on women's poetry, on the long poem and on the literature of the women's movement.
bibliographical_notes: Collected as the final poem of The Dream of a Common Language: Poems 1974-1977 (New York: W. W. Norton, 1978); reprinted in Adrienne Rich's Poetry and Prose (Norton Critical Edition, 1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the possibility of an art made by women out of ordinary materials, and it defines that art against the masculine model of the masterpiece: not transcendence but composition, not brilliance but care. Its second subject is the history of women's dispossession - the 'rootless, dismembered' condition that the poem says it is a difference to know - and the possibility of making a tradition out of what survives. Its third is love, which the poem treats as the ground of the work: the 'you' addressed in its later sections is the lover whose presence makes the room a workshop.
summary: The poem begins in a landscape of hills, birches and a woman walking, and moves inward to a room and to the act of making something: it wants 'to choose a way of life' and to find a composition that has 'nothing to do with eternity, / the striving for greatness, brilliance'. It thinks about the history of women, about being 'rootless, dismembered', and about the difference that knowing this makes. Its central images are a woman's hands, a piece of cloth or a quilt, and the ordinary light of a room; its later passages address a 'you' who is a lover and a listener, and it ends with the two women making 'a whole new poetry beginning here' out of the materials at hand.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as a feminist ars poetica, as a critique of the ideology of genius, and as the culmination of the book's search for a common language; its relation to the tradition of the American long poem, from Whitman and Pound to the postwar sequences, has been discussed, as has its use of the domestic as a ground for aesthetic argument.
research_notes: The first periodical printing was not established from the sources consulted; the poem is dated from its collection in 1978, which is the date the anthology gives.

title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
description: The 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' is an open letter written by Martin Luther King Jr. in the city jail of Birmingham, Alabama, on 16 April 1963, in answer to a statement by eight white Alabama clergymen published as 'A Call for Unity' in the Birmingham News on 12 April. It defends the Birmingham campaign of nonviolent direct action, sets out the difference between just and unjust laws, and criticises white moderates and the white church for urging patience. It was first printed as a pamphlet by the American Friends Service Committee in May 1963 and has become one of the central documents of American political prose.
plot_or_argument: The letter is an argument in five movements, and it is written to be read aloud. Its first movement establishes the writer's standing: King answers the charge of being an outsider by describing the network of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and by asserting the interdependence of all communities - 'I am cognizant of the interrelatedness of all communities and states'. The second movement explains why the campaign could not wait: the four steps of nonviolent action, the broken promises of the Birmingham merchants, and the long list of the reasons why 'we must come to see ... that human progress never rolls in on wheels of inevitability'. The third and most famous movement distinguishes just from unjust laws, using Aquinas, Augustine, Buber and Tillich, and it ends with the claim that one has not only a legal but a moral responsibility to obey just laws and a moral responsibility to disobey unjust ones. The fourth answers the accusation of extremism, turning it into a question - 'will we be extremists for hate or for love?' - and delivers the letter's strongest attack on the white moderate, whose 'shallow understanding' is more frustrating than 'absolute misunderstanding'. The fifth addresses the white church and the praise of the police, and closes on the demonstrators as the South's real heroes. Throughout, the argument is carried by the resources of the sermon: the periodic sentence, the quoted authority, the example, the repetition that builds to a climax.
narrative_structure: An open letter of about seven thousand words in the form of a single continuous argument with no headings, moving from the charge of outsider interference to the justification of direct action, then to the theory of law, then to the charge of extremism, then to the church, and closing with a peroration. Its paragraphs are long and rhythmically organised, and its transitions are managed by direct address ('you may well ask', 'but though I was initially disappointed') so that the reader is kept inside an argument that is also a performance.
meter_and_prosody: The cadences of the Black Baptist sermon: long periodic sentences that rise through parallel clauses to a declaratory close; anaphora and repetition; quotation of Scripture, the Declaration of Independence, Aquinas, Augustine, Buber and Tillich; the rhetorical question answered by the next sentence; concrete example and anecdote set beside abstract argument; a first person that speaks for a movement as well as for a man.
historical_context: Written on 16 April 1963 in the Birmingham city jail, where King was held after his arrest on Good Friday, 12 April, for violating an injunction obtained by the city against demonstrations; he wrote the first part in the margins of a newspaper and continued on scraps of paper supplied through his lawyers, and the text was assembled by Wyatt Tee Walker and Willie Pearl Mackey. It answers 'A Call for Unity', published by eight white Alabama clergymen in the Birmingham News on 12 April 1963, which had called the protests unwise and untimely and urged negotiation in the courts. The complete letter was first published as 'Letter from Birmingham City Jail' by the American Friends Service Committee in May 1963, then in Liberation (June 1963), The Christian Century (12 June 1963) and The New Leader (24 June 1963); The Progressive printed it in July 1963 as 'Tears of Love' and The Atlantic Monthly in August 1963 as 'The Negro Is Your Brother'. King included a version in Why We Can't Wait (1964).
literary_significance: The letter is the most anthologised American prose document of the civil rights movement and one of the central statements of the theory of civil disobedience in English; it was reprinted about fifty times in college readers between 1964 and 1968, it is a standard text in American literature, composition, history, law and theology courses, and its sentence 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere' is among the most quoted in American public speech. Its argument about just and unjust law remains the reference point for every later American debate about the relation of law to justice.
bibliographical_notes: Written in the Birmingham city jail on 16 April 1963; first published in full as Letter from Birmingham City Jail (Philadelphia: American Friends Service Committee, May 1963); printed in Liberation (June 1963), The Christian Century (12 June 1963), The New Leader (24 June 1963), The Progressive (July 1963) and The Atlantic Monthly (August 1963); collected in Why We Can't Wait (New York: Harper & Row, 1964) and in Testament of Hope: The Essential Writings of Martin Luther King, Jr. (1986). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The letter's subjects are the moral obligation to disobey unjust law, the method and theology of nonviolence, and the responsibility of the church and of the moderate. Its argument about law is the most influential thing in it: segregation is unjust not because it is inconvenient but because it denies the personhood of those it segregates, and a law that a minority had no part in making and cannot vote to change is not binding in conscience. Its second subject is time - the clergymen's 'wait' and King's answer that 'justice too long delayed is justice denied' - and its third is the relation of the American present to its founding promises, which the letter quotes against the country that made them.
summary: The letter opens by answering the clergymen's charge that the demonstrations are 'unwise and untimely' and that King is an outsider: he is in Birmingham, he writes, because 'injustice is anywhere ... a threat to justice everywhere'. It then sets out the four steps of a nonviolent campaign - collection of the facts, negotiation, self-purification and direct action - and explains why negotiation had failed. Its central section distinguishes just from unjust laws: 'A just law is a man-made code that squares with the moral law'; 'an unjust law is a code that is out of harmony with the moral law', and segregation is unjust because it distorts the soul and gives the segregator a false sense of superiority. From there it answers the charge of extremism by accepting the word and asking what kind of extremist one will be, criticises the white moderate who prefers 'a negative peace' to 'a positive peace', and reproaches the white church for standing at the side of the status quo. It closes with praise for the demonstrators rather than the police, and with the hope that the South will one day recognise its real heroes.
critical_context: Criticism has read the letter as a sermon, as a work of political theory, as an intervention in the theology of the American church and as a rhetorical performance whose power depends on its occasion; its relation to Thoreau, Gandhi, Augustine and Aquinas has been traced, and its reception - including the fact that the New York Times Magazine declined to publish it - has been studied as a case in the politics of the press. It is also a founding document in the study of American protest literature.
research_notes: The printing history above follows Wikipedia's article on the letter, which is supported by the dealers' and archive records consulted; the sources agree on the May 1963 pamphlet, the June 1963 Liberation printing and the August 1963 Atlantic printing. Quotations are confined to the sentences for which the letter is universally known.

title: The Balloon
description: 'The Balloon' is a short story by Donald Barthelme first published in The New Yorker of 16 April 1966 and collected in Unspeakable Practices, Unnatural Acts (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1968). Its narrator, an unnamed New Yorker, inflates a vast balloon over Manhattan one night; it stays for twenty-two days, the city adapts to it, critics and citizens try to interpret it, and then it is removed as casually as it arrived, having been, the narrator says, 'a spontaneous autobiographical disclosure' occasioned by a lover's absence. It is the most discussed of Barthelme's early stories and the one most often read as a statement of his poetics.
plot_or_argument: The story's plot is minimal and its interest is in the distribution of response. The narrator makes the balloon; the city encounters it; and the encounter sorts the population into types. The children use it - they jump on it, walk across it, take it as a surface - and are entirely without interpretive anxiety. The adults cannot use it: they want it to mean, they propose readings ('bloat' and 'float', dream, responsibility), they write and talk, and their efforts are comic because the balloon's shape changes and because no reading can be confirmed. The authorities try to destroy it, which is also comic, since the balloon is not an object that can be defeated. The narrator watches all this with the detachment of a bureaucrat, and only in the last paragraph does he supply the explanation that everyone has been looking for, and the explanation is a refusal: the balloon was a private gesture, it had no meaning beyond the occasion of his lover's absence, and it is removed as soon as she returns. The story's final line - the fabric stored in West Virginia, awaiting 'some other time of unhappiness' - turns the joke into something else, since it promises that the unhappiness will recur and that the balloon is a renewable resource of the private life.
narrative_structure: A single continuous narrative in the present or recent past, with no scene breaks, moving from the balloon's appearance through the city's responses to the final explanation and removal. The narrative order is chronological but the proportion is inverted: most of the story is given to the public reception and only the last paragraph to the private cause, so that the explanation arrives as an afterthought and has the effect of a joke that also functions as a moral.
meter_and_prosody: A flat, official, faintly bureaucratic prose that reports the fantastic as though it were an incident in a municipal report; long sentences with subordinate clauses and qualifications ('the exact location of which I cannot reveal'); abstract nouns used where a novelist would use description; a complete absence of metaphor in the narration and a positive refusal of symbolism in the ending; dialogue summarised rather than quoted.
historical_context: Written in the mid-1960s, when Barthelme was publishing regularly in The New Yorker and was becoming the most visible of the American writers who had absorbed the examples of Kafka, Beckett, Ionesco and the French New Novel; it appeared in the issue of 16 April 1966 and was collected in Unspeakable Practices, Unnatural Acts (1968), the book that also contains 'The Indian Uprising' and 'Robert Kennedy Saved from Drowning'. It belongs to the moment at which American fiction began to absorb the examples of French theory and of the visual arts, and its balloon has been read as a response to the Minimalist and Pop objects of the New York art world.
literary_significance: 'The Balloon' is the most anthologised of Barthelme's stories apart from 'The School' and the standard text for his account of what a story is; it is a fixture of American short-fiction anthologies and of courses on postmodernism and metafiction, it is widely read as a parable of the reception of avant-garde art, and it is the story most often cited in the criticism that established Barthelme as the central American postmodernist of the 1960s.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The New Yorker, 16 April 1966; collected in Unspeakable Practices, Unnatural Acts (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1968), in Sixty Stories (New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1981) and in Collected Stories (Library of America, 2021). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: 'The Balloon' is a story about the reception of art, and its argument is that the artwork is what cannot be absorbed into the terms its audience brings to it: the balloon is available to the children as a surface, and to the adults only as a demand for meaning that it refuses to satisfy. Its second subject is the city itself, the 'grid of precise, rectangular pathways' against which the balloon's randomness is measured, which makes the story a fable about what escapes urban planning. Its third is the relation of a private occasion to a public object, since the narrator's grief and desire are the balloon's real content and are entirely invisible to the crowd that interprets it.
summary: The story begins in the flat, official tone of a report: 'The balloon, beginning at a point on Fourteenth Street, the exact location of which I cannot reveal, expanded northward all one night, while people were sleeping, until it reached the Park'. The balloon's surface is 'structured' so that a landscape of valleys and knolls is presented, and children jump on it and stroll across it while adults try to read a meaning into its shifting shapes; ideas of 'bloat' and 'float' are introduced, along with concepts of dream and responsibility, and the city authorities attempt to destroy it and fail. There are traffic jams, discussions, 'a number of people' who are 'quite angry', and a general effort to decide what the balloon means. In the final paragraph the narrator meets the woman for whom the balloon was made, on her return from Norway, tells her it is a 'spontaneous autobiographical disclosure' having to do with 'the unease I felt at your absence, and with sexual deprivation', and has it removed; trailer trucks carry away the fabric, which is stored in West Virginia 'awaiting some other time of unhappiness'.
critical_context: Critics have read the story as an ars poetica, as a satire of critical interpretation, as a meditation on the public life of artworks and as an example of Barthelme's 'non-knowing', his term for writing that proceeds without a prior meaning; its relation to Manet's balloon, to the Olympia scandal and to the New York art world of the 1960s has been proposed by critics, and its ending has been central to the argument about whether postmodern fiction can be sentimental.
research_notes: The periodical publication was confirmed from The New Yorker's own archive, which prints the story and gives the issue of 16 April 1966; quotations are short and confined to the passages for which the story is known.

title: The School
description: 'The School' is a very short story by Donald Barthelme, first published in The New Yorker on 17 June 1974 and collected in Amateurs (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1976) and in Sixty Stories (1981). It is narrated by a teacher who tells, in a single breathless monologue, how the plants, animals and people connected with his school kept dying, and how the children finally asked him where they had gone; it ends with the arrival of a new gerbil. It is Barthelme's most accessible story and one of the most widely reprinted American short stories of the postwar decades.
plot_or_argument: The story is a monologue of about twelve hundred words, delivered by a teacher who is trying to give an account of a term in which everything died. Its structure is that of the escalation joke: the pattern is established with the trees ('we had all these children out planting trees'), repeated with the snakes and the herb garden, raised with the tropical fish and with Edgar the puppy, and then raised again - past the point where the joke can be contained - when the children's parents begin to die. The humour is entirely a matter of register: the narrator reports catastrophe in the mild, reasonable, slightly fatuous vocabulary of a progressive school ('we figured that ... that was part of their education', 'that was a blow', 'we were at a loss'), and the gap between the language and the events is the story. The children's questions get sharper as the deaths mount, and the teacher's answers get thinner, until the questions become metaphysical - where did they go, why, what happens to us - and the teacher can only offer the clichés of consolation. The arrival of Helen the gerbil at the end reverses the movement without resolving it: the children are happy, the teacher says he is happy, and the story ends on the possibility that a new life can be received after all the others, which is either a consolation or the grimmest joke in the story.
narrative_structure: A single unbroken monologue in the first person, with no scene divisions and no narrated action outside the speaker's report; its organisation is that of the list, with each death adding a unit to the pattern and each unit slightly exceeding the last. The questions of the children are reported directly and become the story's structural markers, and the final arrival of the gerbil provides the only turn.
meter_and_prosody: Colloquial, rambling, comma-spliced sentences that reproduce the hesitations of speech ('see, because we figured that ... that was part of their education'); the vocabulary of progressive education applied to catastrophe; an absence of metaphor; dialogue reported rather than dramatised; a deadpan delivery that never acknowledges the absurdity of what it is describing.
historical_context: Published in The New Yorker of 17 June 1974, in the year in which Barthelme was teaching at the City College of New York and had published Guilty Pleasures; collected in Amateurs (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1976) and reprinted in Sixty Stories (1981). The story belongs to the period in which Barthelme's short fiction was appearing in the magazine several times a year and in which his work was becoming the standard exhibit of American postmodernism in the classroom.
literary_significance: 'The School' is Barthelme's most anthologised story and one of the most widely reprinted American short stories of the last half-century; it is a standard text in introductions to the short story and to postmodern fiction, it is regularly cited in the criticism of Barthelme's comedy, and its escalation structure is taught as a model of the comic short story. George Saunders has written about it as a pattern story, and it is among the stories through which Barthelme's influence on the American short story of the 1980s and 1990s is traced.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The New Yorker, 17 June 1974; collected in Amateurs (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1976), in Sixty Stories (1981) and in Collected Stories (Library of America, 2021). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is about death, and about the inadequacy of the language in which adults explain it to children: every one of the teacher's consolations is a cliché, and the story's comedy is the comedy of watching a vocabulary fail. Its second subject is the institution - the school as a place where living things are kept, planted and buried - and its third is the children themselves, who move from curiosity to grief to a demand for meaning in the space of a page. The gerbil at the end makes the story a test case for the reader: whether the arrival of a new creature is a promise of continuation or a repetition of the pattern that has just killed everything.
summary: The narrator begins in the middle of things - 'Well, we had all these children out planting trees, see, because we figured that ... that was part of their education' - and reports a series of deaths: the trees the children planted failed; the snakes in the science room died; the herb garden died; the tropical fish died; a puppy called Edgar died; then the children's parents began to die. The children ask questions, and the teacher answers them as best he can, in the language of a liberal education - 'life is like that', 'death is a part of life'. The tone of the monologue stays cheerful and reasonable, and the deaths accumulate with the logic of a joke. At the end Helen, a new gerbil, arrives in a box, and the children are delighted; the narrator says he is delighted too, and the story closes on the last of its questions and the last of its answers.
critical_context: Critics have read the story as an escalation or pattern story, as a parable about the inadequacy of consolation, and as an instance of Barthelme's method of letting a flat voice carry an extreme situation; George Saunders's essay on Barthelme places it in a lineage of pattern stories from Chekhov and Gogol, and the story's ending - the gerbil - has been the focus of the argument about whether Barthelme's fictions are finally affirmative.
research_notes: The periodical date follows the New Yorker archive reference given in the sources consulted; the anthology's date of 1974 is the date of first publication rather than of the collection. Quotations are short and confined to the opening sentences for which the story is known.
